title: Detect a Deadlock in a Wait-For Graph
oneLiner: Given which threads are waiting on which, find every thread that can never finish: the ones in a cycle, and the ones stuck waiting behind it.
keyTakeaway: A deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph. To find every stuck thread, run Kahn's algorithm backwards: a thread waiting on nobody can finish, finishing it releases everyone waiting on it, and whatever never reaches zero outstanding waits is deadlocked, either in a cycle or blocked behind one.
explanation:
This is how a database finds deadlocks. Threads are numbered 0 to n - 1, and each pair [a, b] in waitsFor means thread a is blocked waiting for a lock that thread b holds. A thread can run again only once every thread it waits for has finished and released its locks. Return, in ascending order, every thread that can never finish. If there is no deadlock, return an empty array.

Two kinds of thread are stuck. Threads on a cycle (0 waits for 1, 1 waits for 0) are deadlocked directly. A thread that waits for a deadlocked thread is stuck too, even though it is not on the cycle itself: the thread it needs will never release anything. A thread can also wait on itself, which is what happens when code tries to re-enter a lock that is not reentrant.

Simulate the release order, the way Kahn's topological sort (an algorithm that orders tasks so each comes after everything it depends on, covered later in Data Structures & Algorithms) does. Count how many threads each thread is still waiting for. Every thread with a count of 0 can finish; when one finishes, every thread that was waiting on it has one fewer thing to wait for, and any whose count drops to 0 can finish next. When nothing more can finish, the threads that never got there are exactly the stuck ones. Duplicate pairs never appear in the tests.

Watch the array of outstanding waits below: threads reach 0 one by one and finish, until only the cycle and the thread behind it are left.

visualizationSteps.message: Edges: 0 waits for 1, 1 waits for 2, 2 waits for 1, 3 waits for 4. Each cell is how many threads that thread is still waiting for.
Thread 4 waits for nobody, so it finishes and releases its locks. Now thread 3 can run too.
Thread 3 waits for nobody, so it finishes and releases its locks.
Nothing else can finish. Threads 1 and 2 wait on each other (a cycle) and thread 0 waits behind them. Answer: [0, 1, 2].

recognitionSignals: Tasks, threads or transactions wait on each other, and the question is which of them can ever complete. That is cycle detection on a directed graph.
"Can all of these finish?" is the same question as "is this graph acyclic?", which Kahn's algorithm or a three-colour DFS answers in O(V + E).
gotchas: Edge direction matters: [a, b] means a waits for b, so finishing b is what unblocks a. Build the reverse list (who is waiting on b) to know whose count to decrement.
Threads waiting behind a cycle are stuck too. Returning only the nodes on the cycle misses them.
A self-edge [a, a] is a cycle of length one.
confusableWith: Topological Sort (Patterns track) is the same algorithm. There you return the order; here you return what is left over when the order gets stuck.

complexity.note: Counting waits is one pass over the E edges; then each of the V threads finishes at most once and each edge is decremented at most once. The reverse adjacency list (who waits for whom) is O(V + E).

referenceSolutions.python:
from collections import deque

def find_deadlocked(n, waits_for):
    # waiting_on[a] = how many threads a still waits for; waiters[b] = who waits for b.
    waiting_on = [0] * n
    waiters = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for a, b in waits_for:
        waiting_on[a] += 1
        waiters[b].append(a)

    ready = deque(i for i in range(n) if waiting_on[i] == 0)

    # Finish every thread that can finish; each one unblocks its waiters.
    finished = [False] * n
    while ready:
        t = ready.popleft()
        finished[t] = True
        for w in waiters[t]:
            waiting_on[w] -= 1
            if waiting_on[w] == 0:
                ready.append(w)

    # Whatever never finished is in a cycle or waiting behind one.
    return [i for i in range(n) if not finished[i]]
